title: Introduce idempotent online schema updates and migration checkpointing
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: Our control plane has accumulated multiple ad-hoc schema migrations that require long-running backfills and occasionally introduce downtime or lock contention on high-traffic tables (projects, tenants, audit_events). As we scale Dedicated and Private customers, these interruptions cause customer-visible latency spikes and slow rollout velocity for otherwise small feature changes.

Problem statement: Current migration approach (big SQL files run during deploys or one-off jobs) is brittle: non-idempotent operations, no durable progress tracking, frequent retries re-running work, and occasional full-table locks during index/constraint creation. We need a safe, repeatable migration path that supports: chunked backfills, resumable progress, idempotency, minimal locks, and clear observability + rollback semantics.

Proposal: Build an "idempotent migration runner" + checkpointing table and a set of primitives for safe online schema changes. Design goals: resumable migrations, per-tenant chunked backfills, zero-or-minimal-lock index/constraint creation, and clear cutover semantics for schema swaps.

Key components: 1) migrations.checkpoints table: single-row per-migration key with last_processed_cursor, state (pending/running/done/failed), started_at, last_heartbeat. This is intentionally small and append-only for auditability. 2) Migration runner service: a small Go worker that executes migration steps from a declarative migration manifest. Each step must declare idempotency guarantees (e.g., upsert into target_table where not exists) and support a chunking/cursor mechanism. The runner will persist progress to migrations.checkpoints and expose metrics. 3) Idempotent primitives: SQL templates and helper library for common operations: create_index_concurrently, backfill-in-chunks (cursor-based), safe-add-column-with-default (create nullable col, backfill in chunks, then set NOT NULL in small atomic transaction), primary-key-swap pattern (create new_table, backfill, transactional rename), and FK creation with validation phase (validate -> add constraint with NOT VALID -> validate constraint -> mark as VALID). 4) Telemetry & safety: per-migration dashboards (Progress %, estimated time), per-chunk timing histograms, SLO guardrails (throttle thresholds for CPU/IO, max rows/chunk), and an automatic pause-on-errors mode that requires human approval.

Migration workflow (example): a) Author declarative migration in repo with a manifest and chunking config (batch_size, query to page). b) Create migration record in migrations.checkpoints (runner uses this as trigger). c) Runner picks up migration, claims it (heartbeat) and starts chunked backfills, persisting cursor after each chunk. d) After backfills, runner switches to constraint/index creation using non-blocking approaches (CONCURRENTLY, NOT VALID). e) Final cutover includes a short transactional rename/constraint validation window; a feature flag controls serving logic during cutover if needed.

Success criteria (measurable): - No deploy-induced full-table locks on production during migrations (validated by trace logs and reduced lock wait metrics). - Migrations are resumable after process restarts: runner can resume to last cursor for 95%+ runs. - Reduction in migration-induced incidents by 90% vs historical baseline for last 12 months. - Mean time to complete standard backfill (tenant-ordered job at 10k rows/chunk) is predictable within 25% of estimate.

Trade-offs and decisions: - We considered using pt-online-schema-change / gh-ost but opted for a tailored runner because: we need cross-cloud portability, more visibility into per-tenant backfills, and tighter integration with Redwood feature flags and quotas. - Using CONCURRENTLY and NOT VALID reduces locks but increases complexity in cutover; we'll mitigate with pre-cutover validation steps and staging runs. - Adding a runner increases operational surface area (another service) but centralizes migration safety and enables automated replays.

Rollout plan: Phase 1 (2 weeks): implement migrations.checkpoints table and a minimal runner that can run a trivial chunked backfill job; add metrics and basic dashboard. Phase 2 (3 weeks): implement idempotent primitives (concurrent index, chunked backfill, safe-add-column) and convert one low-risk migration (audit_events schema change) into runner manifest. Phase 3 (4 weeks): run full rehearsal on staging with production-sized data, validate performance, then execute production run in low-traffic window with paging/alerts. Phase 4: incrementally migrate higher-risk schema changes and deprecate the old ad-hoc migration scripts.

Monitoring & alerting: New dashboards for migration progress, chunk latency, DB lock wait events, and runner health. Alerts: runner heartbeat missing >2m, repeated chunk failures >3, lock_wait_seconds 95th pct above baseline, and total migration duration exceeding ETA by 2x.

Rollback & mitigation: Each migration must include a backward-compatible schema path or a documented rollback (drop new column, revert feature flag). The runner supports a "pause and rollback" mode where we can stop further chunks and roll back only if a reversible path exists. Emergency plan: if a migration causes regressions, we will (a) pause runner, (b) enable feature-flag-based fallback for affected endpoints, (c) run a targeted rollback job for the migration manifest.

Risks: - Complexity of developing correct idempotent primitives; mitigated by test harness and integration tests. - Long-running backfills still consume I/O; mitigate via throttling and runbook. - Human error in writing manifests; mitigate via PR code review checklist and CI linting.

Open questions / decisions to make: - Which team owns the runner in steady state (DB infra vs. runtime)? Proposal: Platform infra for development/ops, with runtime on-call for migration execution windows. - How to surface tenant-level throttling for Dedicated customers? Proposal: runner reads tenant QoS policy from config service and applies per-tenant batch_size.

Deliverables: - migrations.checkpoints schema + migration to add it. - migration-runner service (Go) + manifest spec and library of idempotent primitives. - Docs: runbook, manifest authoring guide, PR template, and staging playbook. - Dashboard and SLO alerts.

2025-02-20 - Marcus: Spike complete for migrations.checkpoints table and small PoC runner that can resume a simple cursor-backed backfill (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/2487). Evidence: staging run processed 1M rows in 18m with batch_size=5k.
2025-02-28 - DB Infra review: Prefer use of CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY for indexes and NOT VALID pattern for FK. Added note to manifest spec to include validation_query and safety thresholds.
2025-03-03 - Marcus: Implemented metrics (Prometheus) and a basic dashboard prototype: https://grafana.redwood/internal/d/0000/migration-runner. Added alert for missing heartbeat >2m.
2025-03-04 - Aisha: Scheduled staging rehearsal on 2025-03-18 during Cycle 2025-W11. Assigned follow-ups: add CI linting for manifest, add tenant QoS hook, finalize runbook.
